content.overview: A usable propagation plan works backward from qualified demand and makes assumptions visible. It distinguishes physical capacity from release-ready output and preserves buffers without hiding chronic losses.

vocabulary.definition: The number of identified units a propagation stage can process under defined space, labor and workflow constraints.
An explicit estimate of the proportion expected to reach a defined next-stage criterion.

sections.title: Work backward from qualified demand
sections.body: Start with required handoff quantity and date, then map acclimation, rooting, cutting or establishment stages with their decision points. Calendar days alone do not guarantee readiness.

sections.title: Capacity is stage specific
sections.body: Donor availability, work-area throughput, tray or vessel space, acclimation area and qualified labor can constrain different parts of the system. The smallest effective stage can control total output.

sections.title: Assumptions need owners and revision points
sections.body: Loss, timing and buffer assumptions should identify their source and review date. Large unexplained buffers can conceal poor process capability instead of protecting the crop plan.

workedExamples: A plan for 800 released plants cannot start with 800 cuttings when historical stage losses are material and variable.
Adding rooting space does not increase output when donor harvest capacity is the actual constraint.
commonMistakes: Using one genotype timeline for every line.
Adding buffer without investigating repeated loss.
content.practicalApplication: Create a backward schedule for three genotypes using stated demand, stage capacities, historical yield ranges and hold criteria; identify the bottleneck and the first date the plan must be revised.
content.summary: Propagation planning connects demand to stage-specific capacity, timing, yield assumptions and release evidence while keeping uncertainty visible.
